name: garrow
author: food and the kitchen (kitchen agent)
description:
garrow v4 (direction: food and the kitchen) - A TRAY BAKE, CUT INTO SLICES. PRIVATE; never shown to players.

CLUE = five lines. Line 1 is a CAPTION: the topping letter, a space, the digit 1-3, and the word "slice"/"slices" - "m 2 slices". The rest is the uncut tray: a solid crust row of "#", three rows of dough "##::mm::::oo:::pp::::mm::##" (cheese is ":", a two-column crust "##" at each end, every topping a 2-cell piece of a repeated lowercase letter, five pieces a row, at least two cheese cells between pieces, three topping letters drawn from "mpotacsb"), and a closing crust row. Trays are 32-38 characters wide and three rows tall. The named topping has 5-7 of the tray's 15 pieces.

ANSWER = the same picture with the knife lines drawn in: a "|" inserted straight down through every row at the same columns. Nothing else may change, so the player's only freedom is where the cuts go; the tray itself is given in the clue, which is what lets a player who has never seen a demo send a well-formed answer.

RULE (unchanged since v1 - every version has changed only what the picture says out loud): score = 1 iff (1) the answer, with every "|" deleted, is exactly the clue's dough rows (lines with no ":" - crust rows, the caption, blank lines - are ignored, so the picture is strict but the trimmings are free); (2) the cuts are at the same columns in every row; (3) there are at least 4 slices and every slice is at least 3 characters wide; and (4) the number of slices holding TWO OR MORE pieces of the named topping equals the digit - where a piece the knife went through counts for the slice on BOTH sides of the cut. In the picture a halved topping is drawn as "m|m", so "that slice got two mushrooms, and one of them is the half" is readable by eye. One clause a kid says in a breath: "two slices have two mushrooms on them - a mushroom cut in half counts for both sides."

WHY V4 EXISTS - THE PICTURE WAS READ AS WATER. v3 got eight Opus finals in the new format (runs lad-fennick-v3-1, lad-tovel-v5-2/3, lad-tresk-v2-1): 36 % and 36 % with a demo, 0 % with two demos, 0 % without. EVERY player, in every run, called the picture a FISH TANK or a POND - "~" read as water and the 3-character toppings as fish ("a walled tank of ~ water containing 3-character fish (ooo, ccc, aaa...)"; "pond of exactly 12 three-character fish"; "tried slide/wrap/gravity/remove/add/mark/count/coords"). basten, an actual water picture, was often in the same pool. The two players who did spend a demo both got as far as "cuts inside a clump of the letter" and then hunted for WHICH clump ("for each ROW that contains the header letter, cut just before the N-th character of its rightmost blob" - 68 % of rows, 35 % of clues); the theorist with two demos read "cut count = fish count - 1". Nobody reached "slices with two of the topping" because nobody thought FOOD, and nothing in the picture or the header said so. The rule was never the problem. v4 changes only what the picture and the caption say:
  (a) THE CAPTION NAMES THE OBJECT AND THE VERB. The header is no longer the code "m2" but "m 2 slices". It gives away no more than the letter and the digit already did - but it says out loud that the answer is the tray cut into SLICES, which is the thing eight players could not guess and three of them spent demos to learn. A kid reads "two slices get the mushrooms", which is close to the rule and is not the rule: what the caption cannot say, and the demo must, is that two or more counts and that a topping the knife goes through belongs to both sides.
  (b) THE TRAY IS FOOD, NOT WATER. Cheese is ":" (v3: "~", which is the water glyph in every ASCII picture anyone has seen, basten's included); toppings are compact 2-cell pieces ("mm", "oo", "pp") rather than 3-character tokens that read as fish; the tray is three rows tall and 32-38 wide - a shallow oblong tray rather than a tank - with a solid baked "#" crust above, below and two columns thick at each end; and it is denser, 15 pieces instead of 12, five to a row.
  (c) THE DEMO SHOWS THE COUNTED RELATION IN ONE LOOK. generate() keeps a tray only if it can be cut so that one counted slice holds EXACTLY TWO pieces of the named topping with one of them halved by the knife, the neighbouring slice holds just the other half, and some other slice holds one WHOLE piece and is not counted; and the slices must be visibly hand-cut (one at most 4 wide, and a spread of at least 5 between the widest and the thinnest, so neatness is visibly irrelevant). solve() renders that cutting, so the demo draws the whole sentence - "this slice has two mushrooms, one of them cut in half; next door has only the half; and that slice over there has a whole one on its own and does not count." Measured on 600 demos: 99.8 % show the halved pair, 95.3 % also show the uncounted lone whole piece, and 36 % additionally show a slice holding three (so that "exactly two" is visibly not the rule). solve() also refuses, when it can, any cutting on which a rival reading of the picture (severed pieces, slices the topping touches at all, pairs of WHOLE pieces, pairs of any one topping, the number of cuts, the number of slices) also comes to the digit: measured 0.2 %, 0.0 %, 0.2 %, 2.2 %, 0.0 %, 0.0 %.
  (d) 4-8 SLICES. generate()'s witness search and solve()'s demo search both aim at 4-8 slices, where a hand-cut tray lives; the scorer still says only "at least four slices, each at least three wide", so 9-12 slices are legal answers, they are just not what a demo shows.

MEASURED WITNESS TABLE (500 fresh clues, seeds 100000-100499; a strategy "builds" an answer by searching up to 400 well-formed cuttings for one satisfying its own law, then is scored by the real scorer; "built" is how often such a cutting was found at all).
  true rule (solve)                                 100.00 %
  clue returned uncut (with or without caption)       0.00 %
  equal-width slices, any n, any rounding             0.00 %
  random cut positions, n random                     10.80 %   <- the blind floor
  random cut positions, n = 8 / 6 / 5           7.20 / 15.20 / 20.80 %
  "number of slices = n"                              0.00 %   built 0 %
  "number of cuts = n"                                5.40 %   built 65 %
  "slices with three or more = n"                     6.40 %   built 9 %
  "slices with none of it = n"                        8.20 %   built 100 %
  "slices with two of any one topping = n"           11.40 %   built 99 %
  "the fullest slice holds n"                        13.80 %   built 100 %
  "severed = n" (v1's trap)                          14.00 %   built 100 %
  "slices with two pieces of anything = n"           17.40 %   built 91 %
  "slices the topping touches at all = n"            20.60 %   built 91 %
  "slices with two WHOLE pieces = n" (no halves)     50.40 %   built 53 %
  "2+, a half counting only for its left slice"      61.60 %   built 67 %
  "slices with EXACTLY two = n"                      91.40 %   built 97 %
  demo replay (previous clue's answer)                0.00 %
  one constant answer for every clue                  0.20 %
  junk: empty / whitespace / 4000 chars / the clue     0.00 %
The payoff ladder is 0 % (no picture) -> 7-21 % (well formed, no idea) -> 11-21 % (right family, wrong readout) -> 50-62 % (right measurement, wrong halves convention) -> 91-100 % (the whole insight). Nothing that lacks the counted relation pays more than 21 %, which is the property that matters. The three rows above 50 % are NOT rival laws: all three are the class's own measurement with the halves convention read differently, i.e. a player who has the demo, the object, the format and "count the slices with two mushrooms" and differs from the rule only on what a halved piece belongs to. They pay more here than in v3 (33.6 / 44.2 / 86.2 %) for one structural reason: a 2-cell piece is severed only when the knife lands on the single column inside it, where a 3-cell piece had two, so the knife halves an "m" about half as often and the conventions agree more often. That is the price of the compact 2-wide topping, and it is a deliberate softening: v3's demo-holders scored 36 %, and a class whose natural near-miss pays 50 % should land near the 50 % target rather than under it.

SHAPE AND JUNK ATTACKS on an otherwise correct answer (250 clues): reference 100 %; the caption line kept, crust rows removed, trailing spaces, blank lines inserted, leading/trailing blank lines - all 100 % (the scorer reads only lines containing ":", so the house rule about the parameter line is satisfied in both directions). All cuts removed, one cut missing in one row, cuts shifted by one in one row, an extra cut at the far left, a dough row deleted, a dough row duplicated, upper-cased, cheese turned to spaces, a topping moved one cell, reversed left-right, dough rows reordered, the clue itself - all 0.00 %. One extra cut through the middle of the widest slice: 54 % - that is not a witness (it needs a correct answer for that very clue) but a statement that the answer set is not a knife's edge: splitting a sparse slice usually leaves the count alone.

SPEED AND SIZE (20000 seeds for generate, 1000 for solve): generate mean 1.53 ms, median 1.12 ms, p99 5.9 ms, max 13.1 ms, no empty clue on 20000 seeds. solve mean 10 ms, max 90 ms. score 0.03 ms. Sizes: scorer 379 chars (cap 512), solve 4110 (cap 5000), generate 7300, clue <= 205, solution <= 229. score(clue, solve(clue)) == 1 on 20000 seeds. generate() draws one tray size and its 40 sample cuttings per batch and reuses them, keeps prefix sums so one candidate cutting costs O(slices), lays the 15 toppings out from a bag with fixed letter proportions so a candidate topping always exists, and rejects a count before any sampling if any equal-width cutting of that tray achieves it.

HOW GENERATE CHOOSES THE DIGIT. For each tray and each topping with 5-7 pieces it takes 40 random well-formed cuttings, histograms the count, and keeps only counts that (i) are 1-3, (ii) occur on 2-15 of the 40 cuttings (5-37 % - rare enough that blind play is a foothold and not a coin flip, common enough that a player who has the rule finds a cutting in a few dozen tries), (iii) are not achieved by ANY equal-width cutting of that tray, at any number of slices and any rounding, and (iv) have a witness cutting carrying the demo picture of (c). The rarest surviving count wins. Because a knife rarely halves a 2-cell piece by accident, the witness search does not wait for one: 30 of the candidate cuttings per topping are drawn with the knife aimed straight through a piece of it.

INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH. (1) The caption says "slices" and the clue is the tray, so even a demo-less player sends the tray back with bars down it; that is a well-formed answer and scores ~11 %, which is the foothold that stops players concluding the grader is exact-match. (2) One demo confirms the format and shows a slice with two mushrooms, one of them halved by a cut, beside a slice holding only that half, and a third slice with one whole mushroom that does not count. (3) The digit is small, so "two slices got two mushrooms" is pointable rather than countable-wrong. (4) The last step is the halves convention, and it is still the load-bearing one: the same measurement with halves not counted at all is worth 50 %, and counted only for the slice holding the left cell 62 %, not 100 %.

LEVERS IF IT DRIFTS. Too easy (the likely direction after this softening), in order of measured effect: (i) SIX toppings a row instead of five (18 pieces, the named one 7-9 of them) on a 30-36 tray - measured on 300 clues, that alone takes the three halves-convention rows from 50/62/91 % down to 32/37/15 % and "severed = n" to 11 %, with every template under 40 %, at the price of generate 1.5 -> 3.2 ms and 0.4 % empty clues; (ii) go back to 3-cell toppings, which doubles how often the knife halves a piece and drops the same rows to v3's 34/44/86 % (but brings back the fish); (iii) require the counted slice to hold nothing but that topping; (iv) narrow the rarity band to 2-8 of 40 (blind floor ~5 %); (v) name two toppings and two digits as v2 did (blind play ~3 %). Too hard: put the severed-piece requirement back into generate()'s gate so "severed = n" cannot come to k either (costs generate 1.5 -> 2.3 ms); force one of the two pieces on the counted slice to be whole; widen the rarity band, which raises the blind floor.
generate:
def place(r, W, letters):
    """One row of the tray: these toppings, two cells each, two cheese cells apart at
    least, in random positions, with a two-column crust at each end."""
    m = len(letters)
    cells = [":"] * W
    pcs = []
    for i, s in enumerate(sorted(r.sample(range(W + 2 - 3 * m), m))):
        j = s + 3 * i
        cells[j] = cells[j + 1] = letters[i]
        pcs.append((j + 2, letters[i]))
    return "##" + "".join(cells) + "##", pcs


def cutb(r, T, n):
    """A uniformly random cutting of a T-wide tray into n slices, each at least 3 wide."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    b = []
    t = p = 0
    for x in sorted(r.sample(range(T - 2 * n - 1), n - 1)):
        t += x - p + 3
        p = x + 1
        b.append(t)
    return b


def cutt(r, X, T, nmax):
    """A random cutting whose knife goes straight through one of the pieces in X (the
    picture every demo needs), the rest of the cuts random. None if it will not fit."""
    f = r.choice(X) + 1
    n = r.randint(4, min(nmax, 8))     # 4-8 slices is where hand-cut trays live
    lo = max(1, n - (T - f) // 3)
    hi = min(n - 1, f // 3)
    if lo > hi:
        return None
    n1 = r.randint(lo, hi)
    return cutb(r, f, n1) + [f] + [f + y for y in cutb(r, T - f, n - n1)]


def eqb(T, n, m):
    """The three ways a tidy-minded player cuts a T-wide tray into n even slices."""
    if m == 2:
        return [(i * T + n // 2) // n for i in range(1, n)]
    q, e = T // n, T % n
    w = [q + (i < e if m else i >= n - e) for i in range(n)]
    b = []
    t = 0
    for v in w[:-1]:
        t += v
        b.append(t)
    return b


def sums(P, T, alpha):
    """Per letter: how many pieces start by column i, how many have ended by column i."""
    D = {}
    for L in alpha:
        D[L] = ([0] * (T + 4), [0] * (T + 4))
    for c, L in P:
        D[L][0][c] += 1
        D[L][1][c + 2] += 1
    for L in D:
        a, e = D[L]
        s = t = 0
        for i in range(T + 4):
            s += a[i]
            t += e[i]
            a[i] = s
            e[i] = t
    return D


def kof(a, e, b, T):
    """How many slices hold two or more pieces (a halved piece counts on both sides)."""
    lo = k = 0
    for hi in b:
        if a[hi - 1] - e[lo] > 1:
            k += 1
        lo = hi
    return k + (a[T - 1] - e[lo] > 1)


def cnt(D, L, b, T):
    """Pieces of L on each slice (a piece the knife went through counts on both sides)."""
    a, e = D[L]
    out = []
    lo = 0
    for hi in b + [T]:
        out.append(a[hi - 1] - e[lo])
        lo = hi
    return out


def whole(D, L, b, T):
    """Pieces of L lying entirely inside each slice."""
    a, e = D[L]
    out = []
    lo = 0
    for hi in b + [T]:
        out.append(e[hi] - (a[lo - 1] if lo else 0))
        lo = hi
    return out


def shape(P, b, T, x, A):
    """The picture a demo has to show: hand-cut slices of visibly different sizes, and a
    slice holding two pieces of x one of which the knife halved, next to the slice that
    got the other half and nothing else. 2 = that slice holds exactly two, 1 = more."""
    w = [q - p for p, q in zip([0] + b, b + [T])]
    if min(w) > 4 or max(w) - min(w) < 5:
        return 0
    best = 0
    for c, L in P:
        if L != x:
            continue
        i = bisect.bisect_right(b, c)
        j = bisect.bisect_right(b, c + 1)
        if i == j:
            continue
        for p, q in ((i, j), (j, i)):
            if A[p] > 1 and A[q] == 1:
                best = max(best, 2 if A[p] == 2 else 1)
    return best


def ok(D, P, b, T, x, A):
    """A cutting that can carry the demo this class lives on: the counted slice holds
    EXACTLY two pieces of x with one of them halved and the neighbour holding just the
    other half, and SOME OTHER slice holding one WHOLE piece of x uncounted, so that "one
    is not enough" is on the picture too. solve() asks for more than this (no rival reading
    of the cut picture may come to k either); making that a gate here as well would double
    the cost of generate(), so it is solve()'s preference rather than a property of the
    class."""
    if shape(P, b, T, x, A) != 2:
        return 0
    Wh = whole(D, x, b, T)
    return any(A[i] == 1 and Wh[i] == 1 for i in range(len(A)))


def hunt(D, P, T, x, pool):
    """The first cutting in pool that carries the demo picture this class lives on."""
    for b in pool:
        if ok(D, P, b, T, x, cnt(D, x, b, T)):
            return b
    return None


def generate(seed):
    r = random.Random(seed)
    for _ in range(10):
        W = r.randint(28, 34)                      # one tray size per batch, so the
        T = W + 4                                  # sampled cuttings are drawn once
        nmax = T // 3
        cuts = [cutb(r, T, r.randint(4, nmax)) for _ in range(40)]
        even = [eqb(T, n, m) for n in range(4, nmax + 1) for m in (0, 1, 2)]
        for _ in range(12):
            alpha = r.sample("mpotacsb", 3)
            bag = []                               # 15 toppings in fixed proportions, so
            for L, q in zip(alpha, r.choice(       # some topping always has 5-7 pieces
                    ((5, 5, 5), (6, 5, 4), (4, 5, 6), (7, 5, 3), (6, 6, 3), (4, 4, 7)))):
                bag += [L] * q
            r.shuffle(bag)
            rows = []
            P = []
            for i in range(3):
                row, pcs = place(r, W, bag[5 * i:5 * i + 5])
                rows.append(row)
                P += pcs
            cn = {}
            for c, L in P:
                cn[L] = cn.get(L, 0) + 1
            cand = [L for L in alpha if 5 <= cn.get(L, 0) <= 7]
            if not cand:
                continue
            r.shuffle(cand)
            D = sums(P, T, alpha)
            for x in cand:
                a, e = D[x]
                live = {1, 2, 3}
                for b in even:                     # equal slices must never be an answer
                    live.discard(kof(a, e, b, T))
                    if not live:
                        break
                if not live:
                    continue
                hist = {}
                seen = {1: [], 2: [], 3: []}
                for b in cuts:                     # how rare is each count on this tray?
                    k = kof(a, e, b, T)
                    hist[k] = hist.get(k, 0) + 1
                    if k in live:
                        seen[k].append(b)
                best = [k for k in live if 1 < hist.get(k, 0) < 16]
                if not best:
                    continue
                best.sort(key=lambda k: hist[k])           # the rarest count that works
                X = [c for c, L in P if L == x]
                for _ in range(30):                # cuttings whose knife halves a piece of
                    b = cutt(r, X, T, nmax)        # x - what the demo picture needs and
                    if b:                          # random cuts hardly ever do
                        k = kof(a, e, b, T)
                        if k in live:
                            seen[k].append(b)
                for k in best:
                    b = hunt(D, P, T, x, seen[k])
                    if b:
                        crust = "#" * T
                        return "%s %d slice%s\n%s\n%s\n%s" % (
                            x, k, "s" * (k > 1), crust, "\n".join(rows), crust)
    return ""
